For thirty-two years Ezra Holm kept the light on Gannet Point, the low headland guarding the channel into Kelby. Off the point lie the breakers of Tarrow Shoal; Kelby's harbor lamp burned two miles farther up, and on clear nights both lights were visible from the gallery. In fog a bell was rung by hand for every vessel that passed inside the point, and his daughter Lise kept the logbook. Soon after midnight one November night in 1871, as fog moved in, the schooner Merrow struck the shoal and three of her crew drowned before dawn.

Captain Danby, who had come down the coast on a fair wind, said he had taken Gannet's light for Kelby's harbor lamp and asked that the harbor lamp be painted red. The schooner's owners pressed for a new lens, calling the old one weak and its beam too dim to carry. The pilots of Kelby sent the board a petition: the Merrow's pilot, a stranger, had steered too close to the point, and every pilot working the channel ought to hold a license.

The inquiry found that the shoal had shifted since the charts were made, and it urged a lightship beside Tarrow. Holm had rung the bell all night, and Lise's logbook marks each stroke until dawn. He spent the week after the hearing on the rocks, striking a borrowed church bell into a heavy surf while Lise walked the beach marking where each stroke was drowned out.

The board had little money to spend, and a lightship would have consumed most of it. Its chairman, Amos Reddick, said that a man who had stood thirteen winters on the point knew its weather better than any inquiry, and on the keeper's account of the night the board ordered a heavier bell.

It went up in 1872, low on the rock where Lise's marks showed a stroke carried farthest. In the eighteen years Holm kept the light after that, nothing larger than a rowboat touched Tarrow in fog, and the bell still hangs where he placed it, struck by machine at his old rate of one stroke a minute.

Kellerman's yard closes for good on the first of September, and I spent the last week of August there with my uncle Teodor. The launch Marisol stood on blocks in the shed, out of the water for the first time in forty years. My grandfather built her; Teodor ran her to the island and back for half his life. By Monday every house on the lake had a use to propose for her; by Friday she had a new owner. The marina at Two Harbours sent a cheque, and on Friday he signed it over to the bank. The sailing club had asked in June to teach beginners in her; he said a gift clears no debt, and no beginner boarded her. He had pushed a knife into her garboard plank in June; it went in no quarter inch, and no rot showed along her keel. The islanders would take the county's new boat; the crossing, he said, was no longer his. Petrus rowed over to trade his skiff and outboard; Teodor, who could still slip her single-handed, said a swap brings no money through the gate.

The bank had carried the mortgage since the bad winter, and the sum owed had grown past what a season of repairs could earn. Every other use proposed that week ended at the same wall: pay in September, or the doors would not open again. “The yard outlasts any boat in it,” he said, “and I will not shut these doors to keep one hull in the family.”

The sale drew half the lake to the shed on Friday, and I carried chairs out for people I had never met. He never asked the registry to put her name back on the list. I was not relieved, I was not proud of him, and nothing in it struck me as funny. There would be no crossing to dread in January; I was angry with him all evening, and knew even then the anger was unfair, since the cheque was the yard's one chance.

When Ada Ferris ran the Whitlow schools cross-country course in nineteen minutes and four seconds, the time stood for a fortnight before the committee struck it out. Five reasons were argued at the hearing: a course measured short, a following wind along the ridge, a clock started late, a summer of hill training, and a route diverted around a flooded hollow that cut the last climb.

The hearing found the course short. A surveyor's wheel made it four hundred metres under, and the fault lay in one mismeasured boundary. The ridge gauge read calm, and no wind touched the field. One gun only was fired, and the clock started with it. Ferris trained on no hills that summer and raced unrested. No diversion was made; the hollow was dry and the climb run.

Her school beat Corran that afternoon, defeated them by two points. No pulse throbbed in her throat; she finished breathing easily. No rain struck the marquee, the afternoon staying dry. No path was tramped through the beech wood, which is fenced. The marshals searched no hedges, no boy having strayed. The flags along the ridge marked the halfway point for the runners. Slack on their poles, the flags showed no direction. No marshal was posted at the flags that afternoon. Plain white, they carried no school colours. The flags belong to no village custom, being bought that year.

Future records here will depend on a surveyed course, certified before the season opens. A wind reading at the ridge would record calm air. Two clocks would have shown what one clock showed. The present rules did not suffice on this occasion. A route fixed against alteration is what the field ran.

The committee's decision has my support, and I offer it without qualification. Their two-week delay earns no impatience from me. The decision strikes me as in no way harsh. Thoroughly astonished is how the decision leaves me. Nothing in the decision saddens me on Ferris's account.

The summer I turned fifteen, Grandfather was building the Linnet in his shed at Merrow Point from the plans his father drew sixty years ago. He had raced in the harbor regatta every August of his life, but his hands had grown stiff, so he taught me the steam box, and I bent each plank while he measured it. Mrs. Vale had asked to buy the boat for her grandson to sail on her first visit to the shed.

In July Mr. Corran, who sold us the cedar, rowed across the harbor to look at the hull. He watched Grandfather try to hold a pencil, and then he made his offer: he would finish the Linnet in his yard in time for the regatta and charge only for the varnish. Grandfather said he would think it over, which in our family can mean anything.

One morning a week later the fourth plank split from end to end. Grandfather held his hands up to the light as if they belonged to someone else. “I marked that bevel wrong, Ada,” he said, and he spent the afternoon measuring every frame again, finding each one where the plans put it, while I stood by the steam box and said nothing.

That evening I opened my steam log. On the day I bent the fourth plank he had gone a fair distance up the coast to see Mrs. Vale, and I had pulled the plank out after forty minutes instead of an hour, wanting it on before he came home. I showed him the page. He read it twice. Then he said a repaired plank in a hurried hull would split again in the first heat of August, and that next summer the two of us would rebuild the Linnet properly. The regatta would have to manage without her.

Mrs. Vale found another boat for her grandson, and Grandfather says next summer the way other people say tomorrow. I watched him fumble the latch on the shed door that night, three tries before it caught, and in my room I counted the months to June, and then counted them again.

For six summers Dr. Ines Varela's crew has climbed the same wet slope on Ketil Island before dawn, pushing a gloved arm into storm-petrel burrows to feel whether a chick is inside. The work is tedious and low-tech: a numbered stake at every burrow, a tally sheet in a plastic sleeve, and, by a rule Varela has never relaxed, a scale for every twentieth chick. Mainland colonies of the same bird have been shrinking for twenty years, so anything Ketil does differently is worth a season of somebody's life.

The tally sheets show occupied burrows on the seaward slope rising from 540 in the first season to 870 in the sixth, while the inland slope, walked the same way on the same mornings, ends where it began. The scale shows no difference between the two. Chicks weighed at twenty days old average the same on both slopes in every season of the study.

Varela credits the light rather than the food. In the study's third year the automated station on the headland traded its white lamp for a shielded red one, and the dawn walk changed with it: the grounded fledglings the crew once picked out of the gravel by the dozen, dazzled and unable to lift off again, now number two or three in a whole season. The seaward burrows are precisely the ones whose fledglings must pass beneath the lamp on their first flight out.

Ketil's introduced rats disappeared early in the study, and a visiting biologist has argued ever since that their removal is the whole story. Varela thinks that account fails on its own map: the traps were set in the inland turf, and the inland slope is the ground that gained nothing. Next summer she will visit three other stations that shielded their lamps.

Varela is careful about what a tally sheet can carry. "Six summers is six summers," she tells students who want a headline. "It is a pattern, not a law."

In the spring of 1903 the harbor commission of Alder Cove, a fishing port of nine hundred people, met to settle a question it had deferred for six years. Hollis Vane, the engineer the town had hired the previous autumn, laid his plan before the seven commissioners: to cut a second entrance through the sand spit at Low Point, so that vessels need not beat around the shoal in a southerly wind. His estimate was fourteen thousand dollars, more than Alder Cove had ever borrowed at one time. When the meeting opened, the standing motion was the merchant Amos Kerr's, to do the work in stages over ten years and borrow nothing. Two commissioners, Pell and Danforth, had said nothing at all.

What moved them was neither Vane's drawings nor his figures. A letter came from an Army engineer at the district office, undertaking to match, dollar for dollar, whatever Alder Cove itself spent on the cut. Fourteen thousand dollars had suddenly become seven, and Pell and Danforth voted with Vane that evening.

Kerr's answer was not that the work was useless. It was that the district office had given two other towns the same undertaking within his memory and had honored it in neither of them. He lost, five to two, and the town borrowed in June.

The town dug its own half of the cut in 1904 and stopped. The federal money arrived in 1912 and came to less than a third of the sum promised. The entrance was opened to nine feet and never to the fifteen Vane had drawn; vessels used it in fair weather and avoided it in foul. Whether it would have answered at full depth cannot be said. Vane left in 1908 for a larger post, and the minute book gives the whole business one line.

Over ten years, visits to every public library branch in this city fell — every branch but one. On the east side one small branch held its count steady, and in some years raised it. A team of researchers spent two years finding out why. The answer turned out to be a machine in the corner. The east branch alone stays open into the evening, yet in the month a failed boiler shut it at five with the rest, its daily count did not move. Children whose parents work late do gather there, yet the count stayed as high through the summer holiday, when the schools were shut and those children were at home all day. A rerouted bus line does stop at the branch door, yet when roadworks sent that bus three streets away for a month the count held firm. The same few people have worked that desk for years, yet the busiest month in the record fell while strangers stood at the desk.

The team set the branch against one across the river that had charged for printing after years of giving it away. That branch's count dropped the season the charge began, while here, where the printer queue ran longer than the desk queue, the count held level. The fortnight the printer here stood broken took a third off the daily count, the sharpest fall in the whole record.

After two years the team put the difference down to the printer, a machine nobody had thought worth counting. The branch had been marked for closing in a plan quietly dropped the week the election returns were counted, and nobody had asked why its count held. They admit plainly to surprise that the cheapest of the five explanations was the one left standing at the end. They will not say the finding would hold in another city; they do not fence the result inside this city either; they see nothing fragile in the arrangement; and they make no complaint against the officials who acted on other advice.

The mural on Rowan Street Station's west stair is called the last work of the painter Cecile Mabry. Five accounts of its making circulate: that Mabry painted it herself, that her apprentice Tomas Vane finished it, that three sign-painters worked from her drawing, that the rival Halloran of Preswick was paid for it, and that her brother Emile copied an earlier panel. The station's papers opened last year.

The papers put the brush in the sign-painters' hands. Three were hired from the goods yard, and her drawing issued to them. Mabry never mounted the scaffold, being at Ashe that winter. Vane drew no wages that winter, being at work in Leeds. Halloran of Preswick was paid nothing, and his ledger shows none. Emile signed nothing and appears only as a mourner.

The ground for doubting the old label is a supplier's letter, a reason nobody had. No undercoat lies beneath the paint; plaster took the colour. There is no soil behind that wall, which backs onto the ticket hall. Nothing there serves as a background; figures crowd the wall. Whoever painted it lacked training in drawing, as the hands show. The reopening photograph shows how the concourse was lit. The mural has taken no damage since, so the photograph shows none. The photograph is undated and fixes nothing about the work. No figure in that crowd can be identified. The crowd's reaction goes unrecorded; every face is turned away.

The next step is to look for the squared drawing copyists would have marked. The brushwork of her signed canvases settles nothing; she never touched it. Hunting the walls Vane painted later is idle. Halloran's letters at Preswick prove nothing about a wall he never saw. No earlier panel exists; the design was invented here.

The station's silence since then annoys me more than the finding. My agreement with it is not settled. No reluctance holds me back; I accept it. Curiosity is not what it leaves me. I have no sympathy for anyone it displaces.
